summary:
Visitors to Kansas stand under the United States federal framework. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, defines sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary and requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth; the State Department has stopped processing the X marker, new passports are issued only as M or F from the supporting documents submitted, and passports already bearing an X remain valid until expiry. In November 2025 the Supreme Court allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad. The ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and Lambda Legal maintains guidance on what documentation to consider and how name and gender changes interact with federal records.

State document rules in Kansas tightened with Senate Bill 244, enacted in late February 2026. The law bars updating driver's licences or state identification cards and invalidates existing licences whose gender marker is inconsistent with sex assigned at birth. The Department of Revenue has been mailing written notice, and many holders have already been told that their licence is now invalid. The same statute confines transgender people to facilities designated for their sex assigned at birth and creates new civil and criminal penalties for violations, so a transgender visitor in Kansas should expect to be directed to birth-sex restrooms, locker rooms and other sex-segregated spaces, with penalties attached to refusal.

A legal-risk assessment published on 20 February 2026 moved Kansas from its Worst Laws category to Do Not Travel, the first Do Not Travel designation added in a year. The reclassification follows a law enacted in the same period that lets private individuals sue transgender people encountered in facilities designated for the opposite sex, and the assessment addresses exposure for people crossing into and out of the state by road.

Two transgender men filed Doe v. State of Kansas within days of SB 244's enactment in late February 2026, represented by the ACLU and Ballard Spahr in Douglas County District Court, and they cite fear of violence under the bathroom-restriction and ID-invalidation law.
tangentialFactors:
The Kansas measures sit inside a wider federal pattern. A Movement Advancement Project tally counts state bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings in nine states and one territory, with outright state bans on facility use per gender identity in additional states; 29 states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban, and some states make trans bathroom use a criminal offence in certain circumstances. In April 2025 a transgender student was arrested and handcuffed in a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol in what civil-rights attorneys described as the first known arrest under that state's bathroom-restriction law.

A July 2026 national risk assessment flagged Idaho as the latest Do Not Travel state for trans people, bringing the total to four states so flagged, and reported that the 2026 legislative season continued to degrade trans rights while federal policies drove nationwide trends. Rights groups describe the Kansas statute as a template for other states, with further targeting bills pending in state legislatures.

Screening at US checkpoints carries an outing risk: TSA procedures can involve secondary screening, devices and pat-downs invasive of privacy. Several foreign governments have responded, with advisories issued in April 2025 about trans people travelling to the United States over identity-document and data rules, and at least eight European countries adjusting guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens by March 2025.

Entry carries a separate exposure. In February 2025 the State Department announced a ban on trans athletes entering the United States to compete in women's sports, flagging visa applicants with an internal marking and treating applicants who list a gender other than their assigned sex as grounds for a permanent ban for fraud.

Care and custody risks also bear on a visitor who is detained or becomes unwell. From 2026 the Federal Bureau of Prisons adopted policies mandating conversion therapy for transgender inmates, including cutting hair short, withdrawing hormone medication and substituting psychiatric therapy, and the Bureau stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners held from 2025. In ICE custody, transgender men have reportedly been subjected to forced-labour programmes with refusals met by beatings, solitary confinement and reports of severe sexual abuse. Gender-affirming care for children is banned in 27 states, and October 2025 proposed rules would bar Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18, though several federal measures have been blocked or enjoined in court.
localsOnly:
SB 244 does more than restrict conduct in public buildings. It prevents transgender Kansans from changing markers on birth certificates and driver's licences, and it invalidates existing documents that do not match sex assigned at birth. The Department of Revenue has mailed written notices, and many holders have already received confirmation that their licence is now invalid, which affects identification checks, employment paperwork and interactions with state agencies.

The statute attaches new civil and criminal penalties to violations of its facility provisions, so Kansans face exposure inside the state as well as across state lines. Residents are among those challenging it: two transgender men filed Doe v. State of Kansas in Douglas County District Court within days of enactment, represented by the ACLU and Ballard Spahr, and they cite fear of violence under the bathroom-restriction and ID-invalidation law.

Enforcement pressure is continuing in the legislature. Rights groups describe the Kansas law as a template that other states are copying, and further targeting bills are pending in state legislatures, including in Kansas.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not state the outcome or current status of Doe v. State of Kansas beyond its filing in late February 2026; no ruling, hearing date or injunction is sourced here.

Whether the private right of action that lets individuals sue transgender people in facilities designated for the opposite sex sits inside SB 244 or in a separate statute enacted alongside it is unresolved in these sources. The two are described as connected by date but are not identified as the same measure.

The civil penalties created by SB 244 and the circumstances that make a violation criminal are not specified in the inventory, so the practical line between the two is not sourced.

How far the licence invalidation reaches documents issued by other states, and what a transgender visitor from outside Kansas should expect when presenting an out-of-state licence or ID to Kansas law enforcement, is not addressed by the sources.

Whether any challenge to SB 244 has been filed in federal court, or whether federal constitutional claims are being litigated alongside the Douglas County case, is not sourced.
